events.fact: President Ulysses S. Grant signed the proclamation admitting Colorado as the 38th state, earning it the name 'the Centennial State' for entering the Union in America's hundredth year.
Francis Scott Key, who would write 'The Star-Spangled Banner' after watching the bombardment of Fort McHenry, was born in Frederick County, Maryland.

block: On August 1, 1876, President Ulysses S. Grant signed the proclamation that admitted Colorado as the thirty-eighth state, joining a new commonwealth to the Union in the very year the Republic turned one hundred. On the same day in 1779, Francis Scott Key was born in Frederick County, Maryland, the man whose pen would one day frame the anthem that still asks whether our flag yet waves. A Steadfast citizen takes his place in the long line of those who held the ground their fathers won and sang over it, refusing to let the standard fall while the God who raised this nation still keeps watch over it.

events.fact: Most members of the Continental Congress, beginning with President John Hancock, signed the engrossed parchment copy of the Declaration of Independence in Philadelphia.
The U.S. Mint issued the first Lincoln cent, the first regular American coin to bear the likeness of a president, honoring Abraham Lincoln on the centennial of his birth.

block: On August 2, 1776, the members of the Continental Congress put their names to the engrossed Declaration of Independence, John Hancock signing first with a bold hand and the rest pledging their lives, their fortunes, and their sacred honor to a cause they could not win without Providence. On the same day in 1909, the United States Mint released the first Lincoln cent, setting the face of a fallen president into the common coin so that the humblest pocket might carry the memory of a man who held the Union together. An Obedient citizen submits himself as those signers did to a higher law than his own comfort, binding his name and his labor to the truth and trusting God with the cost.

events.fact: Christopher Columbus set sail from the port of Palos, Spain, with the Nina, the Pinta, and the Santa Maria on the voyage that would reach the Americas that October.
The nuclear submarine USS Nautilus completed the first undersea transit of the geographic North Pole, proving a passage no vessel had ever made beneath the polar ice.

block: On August 3, 1492, Christopher Columbus weighed anchor at Palos half an hour before sunrise, steering three small ships into an open ocean no chart had measured, carried forward by the conviction that a hand greater than his own held the far horizon. On the same day in 1958, the USS Nautilus drove beneath the ice and crossed the geographic North Pole submerged, accomplishing what generations of mariners had deemed impossible. A Steadfast citizen presses into the unknown as these voyagers did, holding his course through dark and uncertain waters because he trusts the God who set the bounds of the sea and goes before His servants.

events.fact: Rear Admiral David G. Farragut led the Union fleet into Mobile Bay, pressing through a Confederate minefield to close one of the last open Southern ports; tradition records his order, 'Damn the torpedoes, full speed ahead.'
The first transatlantic telegraph cable was completed across the ocean floor, and within days carried the first messages between Europe and America.

block: On August 5, 1864, Rear Admiral David Farragut drove his fleet straight into the mines of Mobile Bay, and when his captains faltered he pressed on through the danger to shut one of the last ports open to the Confederacy. On the same day in 1858, after years of failed attempts, the first telegraph cable was at last completed across the floor of the Atlantic, soon binding two continents with words that crossed in moments what ships had carried for weeks. An Obedient citizen advances when duty commands as Farragut did and labors patiently as those cable-layers did, trusting that the God who orders all things rewards the man who obeys the call set before him.

events.fact: The Committee of Detail presented the first full draft of the United States Constitution to the delegates of the Philadelphia Convention for their deliberation.

At the Battle of Oriskany, New York, General Nicholas Herkimer's Tryon County militia, though ambushed and mortally wounding their commander, held their ground and helped break the British siege of Fort Stanwix.

block: On August 6, 1787, the Committee of Detail laid the first complete draft of the Constitution before the assembled delegates in Philadelphia, the framework of ordered liberty under which Americans still live. On the same day in 1777, General Nicholas Herkimer and his Mohawk Valley militia were ambushed near Oriskany, and though their general was struck down and bled to death from his wound, his men stood firm and turned back the force besieging Fort Stanwix. An Obedient citizen honors both the lawmaker who submits his work to careful order and the soldier who holds his post unto death, knowing that God establishes a free people through men who obey their charge and do not flee.

events.fact: Thomas Edison received U.S. Patent 180,857 for his autographic printing process and electric pen, the foundation of the stencil duplicating that became the mimeograph.
President Richard Nixon announced his resignation in a televised address, the first president to resign the office, and power passed peaceably under the Constitution to Vice President Gerald Ford.

block: On August 8, 1876, Thomas Edison secured the patent for his autographic printing and electric pen, the patient fruit of long hours at the workbench that would let ordinary men copy the written word and spread it widely. On the same day in 1974, President Richard Nixon announced his resignation, and the Republic proved its strength as authority passed without a single soldier in the street, exactly as the Constitution provided. An Obedient citizen submits himself to the lawful order whether in the quiet diligence of honest invention or in the humbling of high office, for God has ordained that a free nation stands by men who bow to law above their own will.

events.fact: President James K. Polk signed the act of Congress establishing the Smithsonian Institution, founded with a bequest from James Smithson for the increase and diffusion of knowledge.
Missouri was admitted as the 24th state of the Union, completing the long compromise over its entry.

block: On August 10, 1846, President James Polk signed the act that founded the Smithsonian Institution, turning a foreigner's generous bequest into a lasting house for the increase and diffusion of knowledge among the American people. On the same day in 1821, Missouri entered the Union as the twenty-fourth state, drawing another commonwealth under the settled government of the nation. A Steadfast citizen builds for the generations he will not see, founding institutions of learning and order as a faithful steward of what God has entrusted, that those who come after may inherit a richer and more rooted land.

events.fact: Off Cape Hatteras, wireless operator Theodore Haubner of the SS Arapahoe sent the first recorded American use of the 'SOS' distress signal, summoning the rescue of his disabled steamship.
Andrew Carnegie, the immigrant steelmaker who gave away the bulk of his fortune to build free public libraries across the land, died in Lenox, Massachusetts.

block: On August 11, 1909, the wireless operator of the steamship Arapahoe tapped out the first American 'SOS' off Cape Hatteras, and the new signal of distress brought help across the water to a crippled ship. On the same day in 1919, Andrew Carnegie died, the poor Scottish immigrant who rose by honest industry to command the nation's steel and then poured his fortune into thousands of free libraries for working men and their children. An Obedient citizen heeds the call of his neighbor in distress and pours out his gain for the common good as Carnegie did, obedient to the command of God that we love our neighbor and hold our wealth as a trust rather than a possession.

events.fact: The formal ceremony of annexation was held at Iolani Palace in Honolulu, lowering the Hawaiian flag and raising the Stars and Stripes as the islands joined the United States.
King Philip's War in New England effectively ended when the Wampanoag sachem Metacomet, called King Philip, was killed, bringing a close to one of the bloodiest conflicts the colonies had known.

block: On August 12, 1898, the Hawaiian flag was lowered at Iolani Palace and the Stars and Stripes raised in its place, binding the islands of the Pacific to the American Republic. On the same day in 1676, the long and terrible King Philip's War came to its end in New England with the death of Metacomet, releasing the weary colonies from a struggle that had burned their towns and tested their faith. An Obedient citizen receives both the widening of his nation's borders and the hard-won close of conflict with a humble and ordered heart, submitting his fears and his ambitions alike to the sovereign God who sets the times and the boundaries of every people.

events.fact: Meriwether Lewis met the Shoshone chief Cameahwait, who proved to be the brother of Sacagawea; the reunion secured the horses the Corps of Discovery needed to cross the Rocky Mountains.
American forces under Commodore Robert Stockton and John C. Fremont raised the United States flag over the pueblo of Los Angeles during the Mexican-American War.

block: On August 13, 1805, Meriwether Lewis came upon the Shoshone and found their chief to be the very brother of Sacagawea, a meeting so improbable that it secured the horses the expedition needed to climb the Rockies and reach the Pacific. On the same day in 1846, the American flag was raised over Los Angeles as the long arm of the young Republic reached the western sea. A Steadfast citizen keeps faith with the road set before him through every uncertainty, pressing toward the far country as these explorers and pioneers did, confident that the God who reunites brothers and opens mountain passes will not abandon those who trust Him to the end.

events.fact: President Harry S. Truman announced that Japan had accepted the terms of unconditional surrender, ending the Second World War after nearly four years of American sacrifice.
Congress passed the act establishing the Oregon Territory, extending organized American government over the vast lands of the Pacific Northwest.

block: On August 14, 1945, President Harry Truman stepped before the nation to announce that Japan had surrendered, and a war-weary people who had waited since Pearl Harbor poured into the streets to give thanks that the long ordeal was over. On the same day in 1848, Congress established the Oregon Territory, planting the rule of law and ordered government across the wide reaches of the Northwest. An Obedient citizen endures the long campaign to its appointed end and submits the wild frontier to lawful order, for he knows that the God who rewards faithful obedience brings the weariest war to peace in His own time.

events.fact: The Mayflower set sail from Southampton, England, bearing the Pilgrims who sought to worship God freely and would found Plymouth Colony in the New World.
The Panama Canal opened to traffic when the steamship Ancon made the first official transit, completing the largest American engineering work undertaken to that day.

block: On August 15, 1620, the Mayflower set sail from Southampton carrying the Pilgrims, men and women who left all they knew to worship God according to conscience and to plant a covenant people on a distant shore. On the same day in 1914, the steamship Ancon made the first transit of the Panama Canal, the fruit of immense labor that joined two oceans and bound the commerce of the world together. A Trustworthy citizen proves faithful to the vow he has made, whether the solemn covenant of the Pilgrims with their God or the long promise of a great work carried through to completion, keeping his word as the One who keeps every promise to His people.

events.fact: At the Battle of Bennington, General John Stark's New Hampshire and Massachusetts militia, with Vermont's Green Mountain Boys, crushed a detachment of Burgoyne's army and crippled the British advance toward Saratoga.
The first message passed over the newly completed transatlantic telegraph cable, reading, 'Europe and America are united by telegraphy.'

block: On August 16, 1777, General John Stark and his New Hampshire militia, joined by the Green Mountain Boys, fell upon a foraging column of Burgoyne's army at Bennington and shattered it, stripping the British of the supplies and men they needed and setting the stage for the great victory at Saratoga. On the same day in 1858, the first words crossed the Atlantic cable, declaring that Europe and America were now united by telegraphy. A Steadfast citizen stands firm where he is planted as Stark did and perseveres in a long labor as those cable-builders did, holding the line until the work God appointed is finished and the victory secured.

events.fact: Virginia Dare was born on Roanoke Island, the first child of English parents born in the Americas, in the ill-fated colony that would vanish into history as the Lost Colony.
Meriwether Lewis, who would lead the Corps of Discovery across the continent with William Clark, was born in Albemarle County, Virginia.

block: On August 18, 1587, Virginia Dare was born on Roanoke Island, the first English child born on American soil, a small life entrusted to a wilderness colony that would soon disappear without a trace. On the same day in 1774, Meriwether Lewis was born in the Virginia Piedmont, the man who would one day lead the Corps of Discovery from the Mississippi to the Pacific in obedience to his president's charge. An Obedient citizen receives the calling laid upon him as both these Virginians did, whether the cradle of a frontier colony or the command to open a continent, submitting his whole course to the providence of the God who appoints our times and our places.

events.fact: At the Battle of Fallen Timbers, General 'Mad Anthony' Wayne and his disciplined Legion of the United States defeated a confederacy of Northwest tribes, ending the Northwest Indian War and securing the Ohio country.
Benjamin Harrison, future president of the United States and grandson of President William Henry Harrison, was born in North Bend, Ohio.

block: On August 20, 1794, General Anthony Wayne led his well-drilled Legion to a decisive victory at Fallen Timbers, ending years of bloody warfare on the frontier and opening the Ohio country to settlement under American law. On the same day in 1833, Benjamin Harrison was born in North Bend, Ohio, an heir of a founding family who would himself rise to the presidency. A Loyal citizen gives his steady devotion to his country as Wayne gave his discipline in the field and as Harrison carried forward his family's service, holding fast to the cause and the heritage God has placed in his keeping rather than abandoning his post when ease beckons.

events.fact: Abraham Lincoln and Stephen A. Douglas met at Ottawa, Illinois, for the first of their seven debates, drawing thousands of citizens to weigh the gravest questions of the day in open argument.
President Dwight D. Eisenhower signed the proclamation admitting Hawaii as the 50th state, completing the Union of states as it stands today.

block: On August 21, 1858, Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas stood before twelve thousand citizens at Ottawa, Illinois, opening a series of debates in which a free people reasoned together in the broiling sun over the future of their Republic. On the same day in 1959, President Eisenhower proclaimed Hawaii the fiftieth state, setting the last star in the flag we carry still. A Responsible citizen takes up the weighty duty of self-government as those debaters and their hearers did, studying the questions, casting his vote with care, and answering to God for the stewardship of liberty handed down to him.

events.fact: The American schooner America defeated a fleet of Britain's finest yachts in a race around the Isle of Wight, winning the trophy thereafter known as the America's Cup.
General Stephen W. Kearny proclaimed New Mexico under United States authority at Santa Fe, having taken the territory without firing a shot during the Mexican-American War.

block: On August 22, 1851, the schooner America outsailed the proudest yachts of Britain in a race around the Isle of Wight, the fruit of bold design and seasoned seamanship that won a cup still contested to this day. On the same day in 1846, General Stephen Kearny proclaimed American authority over New Mexico at Santa Fe, bringing a whole territory under ordered government without the firing of a single shot. An Obedient citizen wins his contests by skill within the rules and brings order without needless bloodshed, submitting his strength to lawful ends as a man who answers to the God of peace and not merely to his own ambition.

events.fact: King George III issued his Proclamation of Rebellion, declaring the American colonies in open revolt and refusing the Olive Branch Petition, hardening the colonists' resolve toward independence.
British and allied forces abandoned the siege of Fort Stanwix and withdrew upon the approach of a relief column under Benedict Arnold, securing the Mohawk Valley for the American cause.

block: On August 23, 1775, King George III branded the American colonies in rebellion and slammed shut the door to reconciliation, a stroke that only steeled the colonists to stand for the liberty they would no longer beg for. On the same day in 1777, the enemy abandoned the siege of Fort Stanwix and fled before an approaching relief column, leaving the Mohawk Valley in patriot hands. A Steadfast citizen is not broken by the wrath of the powerful nor moved by the threat of the strong, but holds his ground as those defenders did, trusting that the God who upholds the just will not let the resolute be put to shame.

events.fact: Virginia Dare was baptized into the Church of England on Roanoke Island, one of the first recorded Christian baptisms in what would become the United States.
British troops captured Washington and burned the White House, the Capitol, and other public buildings during the War of 1812, before a summer storm quenched the flames.

block: On August 24, 1587, the infant Virginia Dare was baptized into the church on Roanoke Island, among the first Christian sacraments offered up on the soil of this land, a seed of faith planted in a wilderness that would one day bear a Christian nation. On the same day in 1814, British soldiers put the White House and the Capitol to the torch, and only a sudden storm out of heaven kept the ruin from being total; the buildings rose again and the Republic endured. A Steadfast citizen is neither lifted up by the hope of his beginnings nor cast down by the fire of his trials, but stands fast through ashes and rebuilding alike, knowing the God who waters the first seed also sends the rain that saves His people.

events.fact: President Woodrow Wilson signed the National Park Service Organic Act, creating the agency charged to preserve America's natural and historic places unimpaired for future generations.
Paris was liberated after four years of Nazi occupation as the French 2nd Armored Division and the U.S. 4th Infantry Division entered the city and the German garrison surrendered.

block: On August 25, 1916, President Woodrow Wilson signed the act creating the National Park Service, entrusting to a guardian agency the mountains, forests, and storied grounds of the nation to be kept unspoiled for those yet unborn. On the same day in 1944, American and French soldiers entered Paris and received the surrender of its German garrison, freeing a great city after four long years of occupation. A Steadfast citizen guards what has been committed to him, whether the wild beauty of God's creation or the freedom of an enslaved people, holding the line and keeping the trust until the work of preservation and deliverance is done.

events.fact: Inventor John Fitch was granted a United States patent for the steamboat, having already operated the first regular steamboat service in America on the Delaware River.
Lee de Forest, the inventor of the Audion vacuum tube that made long-range radio broadcasting possible, was born in Council Bluffs, Iowa.

block: On August 26, 1791, John Fitch received a federal patent for the steamboat, a stubborn inventor who had already run the first steam-powered passenger service in America though few would credit him in his own day. On the same day in 1873, Lee de Forest was born in Iowa, the man whose Audion tube would one day carry the human voice across vast distances and open the age of radio. A Steadfast citizen labors on at his calling whether or not the world yet sees its worth, persevering as these inventors did in the long, unglamorous work, confident that the God who gives every good gift honors the faithful hand that does not quit.

events.fact: The Spanish admiral Pedro Menendez de Aviles sighted the coast of Florida on the feast of St. Augustine and named the site accordingly; the settlement he founded days later became the oldest continuous European city in the United States.
Peter Cooper's locomotive Tom Thumb, the first American-built steam engine to run on a common-carrier railroad, made its famous demonstration on the Baltimore and Ohio line.

block: On August 28, 1565, the Spanish admiral Pedro Menendez sighted the Florida shore on the feast day of Saint Augustine and gave the place that name, soon planting there the settlement that endures as the oldest European city in the land. On the same day in 1830, Peter Cooper's little engine Tom Thumb proved on the rails of the Baltimore and Ohio that American steam could pull the freight of a continent, opening the railroad age. A Steadfast citizen lays foundations meant to outlast him as that first settlement did and presses forward the honest work of building as Cooper did, trusting the God who blesses patient labor to raise enduring things from small beginnings.

events.fact: On the night of August 29, General George Washington secretly ferried his entire army of some nine thousand men across the East River from Long Island to Manhattan, escaping the British without the loss of a single life.
Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr., the Boston physician and poet whose verse 'Old Ironsides' saved the frigate USS Constitution from being scrapped, was born in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

block: On August 29, 1776, with his army trapped and the British closing in on Long Island, George Washington spirited nine thousand men across the East River through the night and a covering fog, losing not a single soldier in a deliverance many saw as the hand of God upon the cause of liberty. On the same day in 1809, Oliver Wendell Holmes was born, whose poem 'Old Ironsides' would later rally a nation to save the storied frigate Constitution from the breakers. An Obedient citizen does his duty in the dark hour without panic as Washington did and lifts his voice to preserve what is worthy as Holmes did, trusting that the God who covers His servants in the fog will bring them through to fight another day.

events.fact: The French fleet under Admiral de Grasse arrived in the Chesapeake Bay with twenty-eight ships of the line, the naval move Washington called 'the pivot upon which everything turned,' sealing the trap on Cornwallis at Yorktown.
At the Battle of Richmond, Kentucky, Confederate forces under General Edmund Kirby Smith routed a green Union command, one of the most complete tactical victories of the Civil War.

block: On August 30, 1781, Admiral de Grasse brought his great French fleet into the Chesapeake, honoring the alliance with America and giving Washington the command of the sea that he called the pivot upon which everything turned, the stroke that doomed Cornwallis at Yorktown. On the same day in 1862, raw Union troops were overwhelmed at Richmond, Kentucky, a hard lesson in the cost of facing seasoned men unprepared. A Loyal citizen keeps faith with his allies and his comrades as the French kept faith with a struggling young Republic, standing by his word and his fellows in the day of battle, for the God who is faithful calls His people to a like fidelity.

events.fact: Meriwether Lewis launched his keelboat from Pittsburgh and started down the Ohio River, beginning the journey of the Corps of Discovery that would map a route to the Pacific.
At the Battle of Jonesborough, Union forces under General Sherman severed the last rail line into Atlanta, forcing the city's evacuation and its fall days later.

block: On August 31, 1803, Meriwether Lewis pushed his keelboat into the current at Pittsburgh and began the long descent of the Ohio, the first stroke of an expedition that would carry American feet to the western ocean. On the same day in 1864, General Sherman's men cut the last railroad feeding Atlanta at Jonesborough, and the great city fell, hastening the end of a terrible war. A Trustworthy citizen sets his hand to a charge and sees it through, whether the patient mapping of a wilderness or the hard duty of a soldier, proving faithful in the task entrusted to him as a steward who must one day give account to God.
